title: From Italian Foothills to the Aberdares: Picking Scarpa Hiking Boots in Kenya

content:
Scarpa hiking boots are a sound choice in Kenya if your feet are narrow to average and your hikes involve rock, mud or altitude. The Italian brand's Gore-Tex lined trekking boots, with Vibram rubber soles, suit Mt Kenya, Elephant Hill and Longonot's crater rim, while its lighter suede models cover weekend day hikes near Nairobi.

The hard part is choosing. Scarpa makes everything from climbing shoes to high-altitude mountaineering boots, and the model names (R-Evo, ZG, Mescalito, Terra) mean little until you know what each one is built for. Below you will find what the brand is known for, which lines fit which Kenyan trails, how the boots size up, what to check on a thrifted pair, and how to keep them going for years.

Quick Facts

  • Origin: Scarpa was founded in 1938 in Asolo, in the mountain foothills of north-east Italy.
  • Main hiking lines: R-Evo (the R-Evolution family), ZG TRK, Mescalito TRK and Terra, most with Gore-Tex linings.
  • Soles: Vibram rubber outsoles on all four lines, with deep-lugged trekking soles on the R-Evo, ZG and Mescalito.
  • Fit: generally a precise, close heel hold; the Terra GTX is cut with slightly more toe room.
  • Best Kenyan uses: Mt Kenya treks, the Aberdares, rocky Rift Valley volcanoes and rainy-season day hikes.
  • Resoling: Scarpa lists the ZG TRK GTX and Mescalito TRK GTX as resoleable at approved repairers.

What Is Scarpa Known For?

Scarpa is known for precise, well-built mountain footwear from an Italian company with more than 85 years of boot-making behind it, and Scarpa hiking boots carry that reputation. The brand covers hiking boots, climbing shoes, ski-touring boots and high-altitude mountaineering boots.

The company began in 1938 in Asolo, a hill town in the Veneto region of northern Italy, as a cooperative of local leather craftsmen. The name is an Italian acronym for the "united shoemakers of the Asolo foothills", which is why you sometimes see it written S.C.A.R.P.A. In 1956 the Parisotto brothers took over the business, and the family has stayed closely involved since then. Scarpa's own history page traces how export sales grew through the 1960s and 1970s.

Mountaineers know the name for a different reason. In the 1980s the Polish climber Jerzy Kukuczka wore Scarpa Vega boots on his climbs of the world's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks, and the brand went on to make some of the first plastic Telemark ski boots in the early 1990s. That mountaineering background shows in the hiking range: heel cups that hold firmly, toe caps that protect against rock, and soles designed to bite on loose ground.

For Kenyan hikers, the practical upshot is simple. Scarpa hiking boots are built for terrain that punishes soft footwear: wet roots in the Aberdares, sharp lava on Suswa, and the loose scree above Shipton's Camp on Mt Kenya.

Which Scarpa Hiking Boots Suit Kenyan Trails?

Four lines of Scarpa hiking boots matter most for Kenya: the R-Evo GTX for multi-day treks, the ZG TRK GTX and Mescalito TRK GTX for rough mountain trails, and the Terra GTX for gentler day hikes. All four use Gore-Tex linings and Vibram rubber.

R-Evo GTX (the R-Evolution family)

The R-Evo GTX is Scarpa's comfort-first trekking boot. Scarpa describes it as a boot for technical hikes and multi-day backpacking, with a water-resistant suede upper, a Gore-Tex Performance Comfort lining and a Vibram Biometric Trek sole. Its Sock-Fit DV tongue is a soft-shell panel that wraps the top of the foot, so it suits a wider range of foot shapes than many Italian boots.

On the official R-Evo GTX page, Scarpa lists the pair at 1,320 g in a size 42 and rates it top marks for hill walking and paths, but only middling for steeper mountain walking. That fits Kenyan use well: the Sirimon and Chogoria approaches on Mt Kenya, a wet Elephant Hill climb, or a two-day trek in the Cherangani Hills. Older pairs sold as the R-Evolution GTX come from the same family.

ZG TRK GTX

The ZG TRK GTX is a lighter, more modern trekking boot aimed at challenging trails and long-distance hiking. It pairs a water-repellent suede upper with a PFAS-free Gore-Tex ePE membrane, a 3D TPU toe cap and a sole co-developed with Vibram. Scarpa lists it as resoleable, which matters if you want one pair to last many seasons.

On Kenyan ground, the ZG suits fast day hikes with rocky sections, such as the climb up Ol Donyo Sabuk, the steep start of Longonot, or the Table Mountain ridge in the Aberdares. Its fit icon on Scarpa's site is marked for a medium-volume foot.

Mescalito TRK GTX

The Mescalito TRK GTX takes ideas from Scarpa's approach shoes and puts them into a trekking boot. Scarpa specifies a 1.7-1.9 mm suede upper, a bi-density PU midsole for shock absorption, and a Vibram outsole that grips well on wet rock. The brand pitches it at long hikes and heavier backpacking, and lists it as resoleable.

The Mescalito is the Scarpa to look at if your hikes mix walking with scrambling, for example the rocky top of Oldoinyo Lesatima or the rock band near Point Lenana at 4,985 m.

Terra GTX

The Terra GTX is Scarpa's traditional full-grain leather walking boot. It has a Gore-Tex Extended Comfort lining, an injected PU midsole with a TPU stabiliser, and a Vibram outsole. Scarpa says it fits with slightly more toe room and was designed for lower-level walks and easier hikes.

For Kenya, the Terra is a good fit for forest walks in Karura or Ngong Road Forest, Ngong Hills on a dry day, and rainy-season hikes where leather keeps mud out better than mesh. It is less suited to long scree descents with a heavy pack.

How Do Scarpa Hiking Boots Fit?

Most Scarpa hiking boots fit closely at the heel and midfoot, with a medium-volume forefoot. Hikers with narrow or average feet usually like them; very wide feet often feel pinched, although the R-Evo's sock-style tongue and the Terra's roomier toe box help.

That close heel is the brand's strength. A boot that lets your heel lift will rub on every climb, and on a long descent such as the 1,000-plus metres from Shipton's Camp down the Sirimon route, a loose heel lets your foot slide forward until your toenails hit the front. If heels slip in your current boots, Scarpa hiking boots are worth trying on before you settle on anything else.

Do Scarpa hiking boots run small?

Scarpa hiking boots are sized in EU numbers, and many hikers go up about half a size from their everyday shoe to leave room for a thick hiking sock, as with most hiking boots. Treat that as a guide, not a rule: lasts differ between the R-Evo, ZG, Mescalito and Terra, so always try the exact model.

Check the size label inside the tongue, which normally shows the EU size and often a UK or US size too. The official R-Evo page, for example, lists EU sizes alongside UK 7.5 to 14 for men.

How to try on Scarpa hiking boots in Nairobi

  1. Try boots in the afternoon, when feet have swollen slightly from the day, much as they will by hour four of a hike.
  2. Wear the socks you hike in. A cushioned pair such as our merino wool hiking socks takes up more room than a cotton sock.
  3. With the boot unlaced, slide your foot forward until your toes touch the front. You should fit one finger behind your heel.
  4. Lace firmly, then walk down a ramp or stairs. Your toes should not touch the front, and your heel should stay put.
  5. Stand on your toes and flex the boot. Pressure across the top of the foot usually means the wrong last, not a boot that needs breaking in.

What Should You Check on Second-Hand Scarpa Hiking Boots?

On second-hand Scarpa hiking boots, check five things: lug depth on the sole, the condition of the midsole, cracks in the upper, a firm heel counter and a dry, intact lining. A pair that passes all five can last for years.

Thrifted gear is how most Kenyan hikers get into premium brands. New Italian trekking boots carry a high price in Europe, so quality pre-owned pairs make Scarpa hiking boots realistic on a Nairobi budget. Our guide to buying thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi covers the wider picture; here is what to look at on a Scarpa specifically.

A five-point check for thrifted Scarpa hiking boots

  1. Sole lugs: look at the forefoot and heel. If the lugs are worn nearly flat, the boot will slip on wet murram and grassy slopes. Remember that the ZG and Mescalito can be resoled, so worn rubber on those is not always a deal-breaker.
  2. Midsole: press your thumb into the midsole along the side. It should spring back. Deep creases or crumbling foam mean the cushioning is spent.
  3. Upper: flex the boot and look for cracks across the leather or suede where the toes bend, and for stitching coming loose around the rand.
  4. Heel counter: squeeze the back of the heel. It should feel stiff. A collapsed heel cup loses the snug hold that makes a Scarpa worth buying.
  5. Lining: run your hand inside, feeling for holes near the heel and ankle collar, where Gore-Tex linings wear first. Check the insole too; it is cheap to replace but tells you how hard the boots were used.

How to tell genuine Scarpa hiking boots from fakes

Genuine Scarpa hiking boots usually show the Scarpa name cleanly moulded or stitched, a Vibram logo on the outsole, and a size and model label inside the tongue. Gore-Tex models normally carry Gore-Tex branding on the upper or tongue. Look for even, tight stitching and logos that are sharp, not blurred.

Weight is another clue. A real Gore-Tex trekking boot with a Vibram sole has heft and a stiff, supportive midsole, while many copies feel light and floppy and bend easily in the middle. These are general signs only; when in doubt, compare the boot against photos on Scarpa's official site.

Scarpa, Lowa or Keen: Which Brand Should You Pick?

Pick Scarpa for a precise heel hold on rocky, technical ground, Lowa for an all-round fit and long multi-day treks, and Keen if your feet are wide. All three make Gore-Tex or waterproof mid boots that handle Kenya's rainy seasons.

The Lowa Renegade EVO GTX Mid is the closest rival to a Scarpa R-Evo: both are mid-cut, Gore-Tex lined and built for trekking. The Lowa is usually a touch roomier through the midfoot, while the Scarpa feels more locked in at the heel. Lowa's range sits on our Lowa brand page.

The Keen Targhee Mid Waterproof goes the other way, with a wide toe box and a big rubber toe bumper. If you have tried Scarpa hiking boots and felt squeezed across the toes, our Keen hiking boots guide explains why Keen suits broad feet. For a side-by-side look at every major label, see our roundup of the best hiking boot brands in Kenya.

A fair way to decide: if you mostly hike Ngong Hills, Karura and Ol Donyo Sabuk, any of the three brands will do the job and fit matters more than the badge. If you are training for Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro, choose whichever brand holds your heel firmly with a full pack, and walk in it for at least a month before the climb.

How Do You Care for Scarpa Hiking Boots in Kenya's Dust and Mud?

Care for Scarpa hiking boots by brushing off mud after every hike, rinsing with clean water, drying them slowly at room temperature, and treating suede or leather with a product made for Gore-Tex boots. Never dry them beside a jiko, fire or heater.

Red murram and volcanic dust work into stitching and suede, and dried mud pulls moisture out of leather as it hardens. A soft brush and a bucket of water at the end of a Longonot or Elephant Hill day will add seasons to any pair of Scarpa hiking boots. Take the insoles out and stuff the boots with newspaper so they dry from the inside overnight.

Heat is the biggest enemy. Leather shrinks and cracks when it dries too fast, and the glue holding the sole can soften. On a campsite at Mt Kenya's Old Moses or Shipton's, it is tempting to put boots by the stove; keep them under the tent fly instead and wear dry socks to bed.

Every few months, or when water stops beading on the surface, re-proof the boots. Use a spray for suede models such as the R-Evo, ZG and Mescalito, and a wax or cream suited to Gore-Tex for full-grain leather like the Terra. Clean the boots first, apply the treatment while the leather is slightly damp, then let it dry naturally.

Pro Tips for Scarpa Owners

  • Break new or new-to-you boots in on Karura Forest's trails before taking them up a mountain.
  • Use the lace lock at the ankle to keep the forefoot relaxed and the heel snug on long descents.
  • Add waterproof leg gaiters for the Aberdares bogs and Mt Kenya's Vertical Bog; Gore-Tex cannot stop water pouring in over the collar.
  • Carry a spare pair of socks on rainy-season hikes; dry feet blister far less than wet ones.
  • Store boots in a dry, shaded spot, not a sealed plastic bag, so the leather can breathe.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Scarpa hiking boots good for Mt Kenya?

Scarpa hiking boots are a strong match for Mt Kenya, especially the R-Evo GTX and Mescalito TRK GTX. Both have Gore-Tex linings for the wet lower forest and moorland, Vibram soles for scree, and a firm heel for the long descent. Pair them with warm socks and gaiters, because nights at Shipton's Camp drop below freezing and the Vertical Bog on the Naro Moru route is very wet.

Is Scarpa better than Lowa?

Scarpa is not better than Lowa overall; the two brands simply fit differently. Scarpa hiking boots usually hold the heel more tightly and feel more precise on rock, while Lowa boots such as the Renegade tend to feel a little roomier through the midfoot. Both use Gore-Tex and Vibram on their main trekking models. Choose the one that keeps your heel still and your toes free on a downhill slope.

Can I wear Scarpa hiking boots on day hikes around Nairobi?

Scarpa hiking boots work well on day hikes around Nairobi, though a heavy trekking model can feel warm on a dry, hot Ngong Hills ridge. The Terra GTX and ZG TRK GTX are the lighter choices for Karura, Ol Donyo Sabuk and Longonot. Save stiffer boots for rainy-season hikes, rocky volcanoes and anything above 3,000 m, where support and grip earn their weight.

How long do Scarpa hiking boots last?

Scarpa hiking boots can last many years of regular hiking if they are cleaned, dried slowly and re-proofed. The sole rubber usually wears out first. Scarpa lists the ZG TRK GTX and Mescalito TRK GTX as resoleable, so an upper in good condition can get a fresh sole instead of being thrown away. Heat damage and dried-on mud shorten a boot's life faster than mileage does.

Do Scarpa hiking boots need breaking in?

Scarpa hiking boots with suede uppers, such as the R-Evo and ZG, need only light breaking in: a few short walks around your estate or Karura Forest. Full-grain leather boots like the Terra take longer to soften. Whatever the model, never take brand-new or newly bought second-hand boots straight onto a long climb; walk at least 20-30 km in them first so any hot spots show up early.

Final Thoughts

Italian craft, Gore-Tex linings and a heel that stays where it should are what you pay for with Scarpa. Match the line to the trail: R-Evo or Mescalito for Mt Kenya and rocky scrambles, ZG for fast rocky day hikes, Terra for forest walks and mud. Then let fit decide.
